thread.title: Fitbit Stock Soared Today. Does That Mean It's a Health-Care Company Now?

title: Fitbit Stock Soared Today. Does That Mean It's a Health-Care Company Now?
text:
Fitbit Stock Soared Today. Does That Mean It’s a Health-Care Company Now? By Updated Nov. 1, 2018 4:08 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Rich Fury/Getty Images for Fitbit Text size
Fitbit stock soared on Thursday morning as the company reported encouraging third-quarter numbers and pointed investors toward more of the same to finish the year. But for investors who believe its destiny lies beyond being “just” a device maker, the most important news may come in 2019.
For now, though, investors seem happy to applaud its latest results and its updated near-term outlook. The smartwatch and fitness-tracker company turned in a quarterly profit (using nonstandard accounting) after reporting a loss last year, then told investors to expect another one in the fourth quarter.
And the response—Fitbit stock (ticker: FIT) rose more than 25% to just below $6 per share in Thursday trading—suggests some degree of belief that Fitbit, still well off its post-IPO highs, has turned the corner. Fitbit stock was positioned to record its largest single-day percentage increase ever, according to Dow Jones data.
Fitbit was essentially forced to evolve from a tracker-device maker to a smartwatch company as Apple ’s (AAPL) Watch essentially jump-started the category. Fitbit represented more than 9% of all wearables shipments worldwide in the second quarter, according to IDC, helped by its Versa watch.
As Fitbit has added smartwatches to its lineup, they have come to represent about half of its revenue in a short time. Consequently, Fitbit’s overall average selling prices have risen—but gross margins have slipped. (Though that has been helped a bit, management says, by better device quality that has helped warranty-related costs.) Newsletter Sign-up
Management said gross margins, which fell year over year in the third quarter, could improve in the fourth quarter—its most financially important—thanks in part to its latest tracker, which arrived in the middle of the last quarter . Cleaner inventory, meanwhile, has meant fewer promotions on older products, CFO Ron Kisling told Barron’s in an interview on Wednesday.
The key to unlocking the next stage of growth at Fitbit may come from the health-care business, since partnerships with that industry could lead to revenue opportunities from direct sales to health plans and data analysis. Its purchase of a company called Twine Health earlier this year led to the launch of Fitbit Care , a platform that Humana (HUM) now uses to offer coaching and information to its members.
Right now, health care makes up less than 10% of Fitbit revenue. (The company trumpeted 26% year-over-year growth, however, in its release on Wednesday.) “We’re trying to shift our model away from being purely device-centric to being a more solutions-oriented business,” CEO James Park said on a conference call, a transcript of which was available on Seeking Alpha .
That, Park said, should mean both device sales and per user revenue from participating organizations. (He said to expect “predicable revenue streams,” rather than spikes, as that business grows.) It might also eventually yield some kind of results-related revenue: On Wednesday, Park suggested ”potentially some sharing in cost savings, as well.”
Fitbit is still fairly close-lipped about the health-care business, though Park told Barron’s that as it grows, investors can expect “more transparency” next year.
Wedbush analyst Michael Pachter reiterated his Outpeform rating on Thursday. His $6.50 price target is right at Factset’s current average, and he sees the new Charge 3 tracker as both an appealing consumer device and an option for health-care-related users. Recommended Reading
